name: Ben Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Gerry Walsh, a small builder in our town, and I've been with him twenty-two years. We do extensions, loft conversions, new roofs, kitchens, whatever people need on their houses. Right now I'm framing a loft for a young couple on Chapel Street, cutting joists and putting in a staircase. I like that people know me, I've done work in half the houses on my road. What wears me out is the ladders, and the paperwork Gerry's started asking for.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Twenty-two years with Gerry. Tell me a bit about life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Rosa works mornings in the bakery on the square. We've three grown children, Miguel's a plumber, Ana's at home with three little ones, and Luis has just joined the police. Sunday is church and then lunch at ours, all of them, it's loud. Money's not much, we rent and there's maybe two weeks put by, and there's no other builder round here who'd take on a man my age. I don't use computers, Rosa does the bills on her phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I could have told them that. You can't swing a hammer with a computer. After church I'd have a laugh about it with the other men.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good. Nothing changes, Gerry keeps the work coming, people keep wanting extensions. I'd just like a bit more pay, but that's not the computer's fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I've always done. Turn up at half seven, do a proper job, go home. I'd hope to work with Gerry until he retires, and then see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like nothing to report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Gerry's paperwork. What's that about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerry's daughter Clare does his office now, and she wants photos of every job on a phone, and forms for health and safety. I take the photos on Gerry's phone because I haven't got one that does it. It feels like we're building for the forms, not the customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when Gerry retires?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the question. He's 66. Maybe Clare keeps it going with somebody, maybe it closes. I'd ask around the church, people always need things fixed. I'd be all right doing small jobs.

S0.say: I could have told them that, you can't swing a hammer with a computer. I'd laugh about it with the men after church.
S0.think: It's good for me, nothing changes and the work keeps coming. I'd like more pay, but that's not the computer's fault.
S0.do: Keeps working for Gerry as he always has, starting at half seven and doing a proper job. Hopes to stay until Gerry retires and then see what comes.
S0.quote: It feels like we're building for the forms, not the customer.
S0.fieldNote: Ben is settled and content in this picture, with his only gripe being paperwork. His bigger hidden risk is his 66-year-old boss retiring, not AI. He leans on church and community as his safety net from the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will always want a man they know in their house. Big firms might use robots, but not here. I'd say that after church and at the builder's merchant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I wonder. Clare's already talking about using a computer for quotes, and if the young couples start going to a big firm with a cheaper robot price, Gerry loses out. But most of our customers are people who know us, and they don't want a machine in their loft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't change much, I'd keep my head down and keep working. I'm not going to learn computers at this age, I'd leave that to Clare. I'd wait and see how it goes with Gerry's customers before doing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, if I'm honest. Like a draught under the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said customers know you. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Dawson on Mill Road, I built her extension in 2009 and her daughter's in 2021. When her gutter came down last year she rang Gerry and asked for me by name. A robot firm from the city doesn't get those calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You won't learn computers. If Gerry asked you to, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerry wouldn't ask, he knows me. If Clare asked, I'd tell her politely that my job is the timber and hers is the screen. That's how it's worked for twenty years and it works fine.

S1.say: People will always want a man they know in their house. Big firms might use robots, but not here.
S1.think: Clare's already talking about computer quotes, and cheaper robot prices from big firms could take young customers. But most of our customers know us and don't want a machine in their loft.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and keeps working, refusing to learn computers and leaving that to Gerry's daughter. Waits to see how Gerry's customers respond before doing anything.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like a draught under the door.
S1.quote: A robot firm from the city doesn't get those calls.
S1.fieldNote: He trusts local loyalty to protect him and has a real story to back it up. He's firm about not learning computers and sees the screen as someone else's job. A quiet worry about younger customers shows he isn't as sure as he says in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big tech companies have got too much power, and they've done this for their own pockets. I'd say people should keep hiring local men. I'd say it at church, at the pub, anywhere, but not online, I'm not on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be hard. I'd be 60, two weeks of money, and Gerry probably packing it in because he can't compete. My knees won't let me do much else, and there's nobody else round here who'd hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as long as anyone would pay me, Gerry or the neighbours. I'd do small jobs for church families and people I know, fixing doors, sheds, gates, for cash. Rosa and I would cut right back, and I'd lean on Miguel if I had to, he's doing well with the plumbing. I wouldn't go on benefits unless there was nothing left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that, with only two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake, and I'd pray a lot more than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not benefits, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my father never took a penny from anyone and I won't either, not while I can stand. It's not that I think badly of people who do. It's that I'd feel I'd stopped being a man who provides. Family first, then church, then, if God wills it, the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years before it arrives. What would you do with them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work, same as always. Maybe ask Gerry for every hour going. I wouldn't change who I am in two years, I can't learn computers that fast and I don't want to. I'd just try to be the one people ring.

S2.say: Big tech companies have too much power and did this for their own pockets, so people should keep hiring local men. I'd say it at church and the pub, not online.
S2.think: At 60, with two weeks of money and Gerry likely packing it in, it'd be hard. My knees limit me and nobody else round here would hire me.
S2.do: Keeps working for anyone who will pay and does cash jobs for church families and neighbours. Cuts right back with Rosa, leans on his son Miguel if needed, and refuses benefits unless nothing else is left.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake and praying more than usual.
S2.quote: Family first, then church, then, if God wills it, the government.
S2.fieldNote: He blames big tech for grabbing power rather than government for failing to regulate. His order of support is clear: work, family, church, and only then the state. He won't change himself in two years and says so, which leaves him exposed and losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, keep hiring local. I'd also say the young ones should get a proper apprenticeship, not sit at screens. I'd say it to the men after church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to 63. If Gerry holds on that long and there are still people who want a man they know, I might get through. Then a couple of years of odd jobs to the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working with Gerry and start building up the odd jobs on the side now, so there's a list of people who ring me when the time comes. I'd try to put away the cash from those jobs, maybe forty a week. I still wouldn't learn computers, but I'd let Luis set up a phone so people can text me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that feel compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's still coming, but I can see a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd let Luis set up a phone. That's a change from before. What made you shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough that I'd need people to find me without Gerry. A phone that takes texts isn't computers, it's just a phone. Luis would show me twice and then get impatient, but I'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rosa say about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say put the cash in the bank, not the biscuit tin. She's right, the biscuit tin has a habit of paying for grandchildren's birthdays. Rosa's the sensible one, always has been.

S3.say: Keep hiring local, and the young ones should get proper apprenticeships, not sit at screens. I'd say it to the men after church.
S3.think: By 63, if Gerry holds on and people still want a man they know, I might get through. Then a couple of years of odd jobs to the pension.
S3.do: Keeps working with Gerry and builds up a list of side jobs now for when the time comes. Saves about forty a week from the cash work, and lets his son set up a simple phone so people can text him.
S3.feel: Anxious, but able to see a way through.
S3.quote: She's right, the biscuit tin has a habit of paying for grandchildren's birthdays.
S3.fieldNote: Five years nudges him to one small change, a phone for texts, which he carefully frames as not being computers. His plan is to build a local reputation for odd jobs. He keeps returning to apprenticeships as the right path for the young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, and half of what they say won't happen. I'd tell the young ones to learn a trade with their hands. I'd say it at the Sunday table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'm 68, so I'd be retired or doing odd jobs anyway. It's my grandchildren I'd think about. Ana's eldest is twelve, he'd be looking for work right when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade's warning, what would you actually do, now and in the first year after it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working with Gerry like now, no changes. I'd wait and see what happens, because ten years is a long time and things never go the way the experts say. I'd tell Ana's eldest to look at apprenticeships when he's sixteen, but that's his choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the grandchildren, but for me, fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell your grandson to look at an apprenticeship. What if robots are doing those trades too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know, honestly. I'd still say learn to do something real with your hands, because a man who can fix things is never useless. But I wouldn't know what to tell him beyond that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do with ten years that you wouldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pray for the young ones, mostly. For me, ten years means I'm out before it comes, so I'd stay as I am. It's selfish, maybe, but at my age you look after what's in front of you.

S4.say: Ten years is a long way off and half of what they say won't happen. I'd tell the young ones at the Sunday table to learn a trade with their hands.
S4.think: At 68 I'd be retired or doing odd jobs anyway. It's my grandchildren I'd think about, especially Ana's eldest, who'd be looking for work right when it hits.
S4.do: Keeps working with Gerry with no changes and waits to see what happens. Suggests apprenticeships to his eldest grandson while leaving the choice to him.
S4.feel: Uneasy for the grandchildren, fine for himself.
S4.quote: I'd still say learn to do something real with your hands, because a man who can fix things is never useless.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he simply plans to stay as he is, since he'll be past pension age. His advice to the next generation is apprenticeships, though he admits he doesn't know if that's enough. He's honest about not knowing what to tell his grandson.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, too quick for a man like me. What would help is if people kept choosing local tradesmen, and if the government made it easier for small firms like Gerry's to keep going instead of piling forms on them. And proper apprenticeships for the young, paid, so they learn from men like me while we're still here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Whatever comes, I believe we're looked after if we look after each other. That's not an answer for the economists, but it's how I'd get through it.

headlineQuote: Whatever comes, I believe we're looked after if we look after each other.
portrait: Ben Diaz is a 58-year-old carpenter who has worked twenty-two years for a small-town builder, framing lofts and extensions in houses where people ask for him by name. He rents, has two weeks of savings, doesn't use computers and puts work, family and church ahead of any government help. He's calm in the Plateau and only uneasy in Steady Disruption, trusting local loyalty. AGI by 2028 alarms him because his boss would likely close and he won't change himself in two years, while five years nudges him to get a phone for odd-job texts. With ten years he plans no changes and worries for his grandchildren instead.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would be too quick for a man like him.
whatWouldHelp: People continuing to choose local tradesmen, less paperwork for small firms, and paid apprenticeships so the young learn from older tradesmen.
